newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges Blair work fast on Northern Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges Blair work fast on Northern Ireland.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday urged Britain's new prime minister Tony Blair to "take up the torch" and reignite the stalled Northern Ireland peace process now that British elections are over.
"It's high time and I can tell you that's what the people of Northern Ireland want," Clinton told reporters.

The president commented for the first time on Britain's election Thursday in which Blair's Labour Party scored a stunning landslide victory that ousted British Prime Minister John Major and his Conservatives.

Clinton said he was impressed with the way Major encouraged the start of the peace process in Northern Ireland, where the Irish Republican Army has waged a 28-year campaign to force an end to British rule.

Guerrilla violence and political wrangling have blocked the revival of the peace process in the province, where more than 3,000 people have died over the last three decades in fighting between Protestants who want to stay part of Britain and Catholics who want the region to be united with Ireland.

"I hope and pray now that the British election is over that Prime Minister Blair will take up the torch, the IRA will declare a ceasefire and they can get back on the road to resolving their problems," said Clinton, who visited Northern Ireland in 1995.
Clinton said he was looking forward to working with Blair, who he described as an exciting and able man. "I like him very much," he said.

But he had much praise for Major, with whom he worked closely over the last four years. He said Major was willing to take tough decisions, and in particular praised him for working with Washington to help bring the Bosnian conflict to an end.
"The people of the United States and the people of Great Britain should know that John Major represented their nation very well in the world," he said.
He said Major's Conservatives had a long run in power, but that "nothing lasts forever."
"But I hope that the British people will always feel a great deal of pride in what they did and the way they related to the rest of the world in his stewardship," Clinton said.

Some of Clinton's former political advisers, including his former pollster Stan Greenberg, served discreetly as campaign advisers to Blair and there was criticism in Britain that Blair ran a Clinton-style campaign. The White House said Friday this charge reflected "less-than-sophisticated punditry."
